This post aptly captures the "limitations" of formal verification and how they apply to the recent proof of RH. I wish everyone chiming into the LEAN proof of RH discussion consider these limitations.

https://tagide.com/blog/research/formal-verification-is-not-the-silver-bullet/ via @crista

#software #formalverification #math #lean

The Lean and Mathlib communities have released a joint statement on the Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library of 17 million lines of code. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities worked together to verify it. The joint statement certifies the proof as correct and describes how it meets all necessary verification criteria.

Congratulations to Levent on this achievement, and thank you to everyone in the community who contributed time and resources to the verification.

Full statement: https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/riemann-hypothesis/

#Lean #Mathlib #RiemannHypothesis #FormalVerification

item.description:
Anthropic employee claims general proof of the Riemann Hypothesis [pdf] alpo.ge · 934 points · 578 comments · HN thread

TL;DR Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted a PDF claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, developed with Claude, and extending to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The argument is roughly 250,000 pages on paper, and its Lean formalization (about 17 million lines in 175,000+ files, roughly 1 GB) is linked as 14 archive parts rather than a readable writeup. Commenters are excited but mostly insist on independent verification before accepting the claim.

  • Alpöge says he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and that the method also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, with the Extended Riemann Hypothesis expected with more time.
  • The full argument was formalized in Lean; the PDF links 14 archive parts (lean.tar.gz.part01 to part14) rather than a human-readable write-up, which he says would be an unreadable 250,000-page document.
  • He describes Claude's role as doing much of the technical work while he guided the approach, and gives a timeline of about 20 steps ending with GRH on 11/16/26.
  • The announcement came shortly after Anthropic's IPO; Alpöge says he finished the proof before the IPO and chose to wait to announce, and he denies that timing was intended.
  • Commenters note the Lean statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is taken from Mathlib, so verification mainly depends on that statement being faithful and the kernel being sound.
  • Alpöge previously worked with OpenAI's Navier-Stokes effort, which drew criticism; this announcement is seen as more deferential in tone.

Discussion The thread is large and split between excitement about a possible milestone in AI-assisted mathematics and skepticism about hype, verification, and the anthropomorphic language in the write-up. Many commenters focus on whether the Lean proof is checkable, whether the statement is correctly formalized, and whether the proof can be understood by humans at all. Others debate what AI progress means, whether the result is 'AI' or 'human plus AI', and whether it matters practically since RH has few direct applications. The mood is mostly impressed and somewhat anxious, with a noticeable undercurrent of distrust toward Anthropic's motives and timing.

  • Impressive milestone, but wait for expert verification (most): Most commenters find the claim exciting and plausible given the Lean formalization, but say mathematicians must review the proof and the statement before accepting it. Several cite past false claims such as Mochizuki and early Wiles gaps.
  • Lean verification makes it highly credible (many): A substantial group argues the machine-checked Lean proof, the standard Mathlib statement of RH, and independent kernels make an error unlikely, so the main remaining check is that the statement is faithful.
  • Credentials alone are not verification (some): Some push back on the 'if he says so, it is so' framing, arguing that an authority's word should not substitute for checking, even though his background is respected.
  • AI is now clearly achieving research-level results (many): Many see this as evidence that frontier models are now capable of major mathematical discovery, and that human-plus-AI workflows will keep producing results.
  • Skeptical that AI results mean general intelligence (some): Others argue that solving verifiable problems does not imply general or superintelligence, noting jagged capabilities and that the work needed top human expertise.
  • Concern about understanding and the future of human mathematics (some): A recurring worry is that a 250,000-page proof no human can read changes mathematics from understanding to trust, and that the field's social structure for training mathematicians is at risk.
  • Dislike of the anthropomorphic and promotional tone (a few): Some find the phrasing about Claude 'flying and dancing' cringeworthy, and suspect the timing relative to the IPO was meant to boost the stock, though others defend the language as genuine enthusiasm.

Links from the comments

  • A commenter's repo for building the Lean code, noting a lake build is running (no comparator added).
  • DeepMind's formal-conjectures collection of human-written Lean statements, cited as a basis for checking statements like Navier-Stokes and GRH.
  • Kevin Buzzard's post on how to check that an untrusted Lean proof does not exploit axioms or kernel bugs.
  • Mathlib documentation for the formal statement of the Riemann zeta and Riemann Hypothesis that the proof is checked against.
  • Linked result: a conditional proof of Goldbach-type statements assuming GRH, relevant to what GRH would imply.

Lean 4.36.0 has been released. This is mostly a consolidation release, with 222 changes, including 30 performance improvements.

From the highlights:
• Much of the work went into performance, including keeping the type class cache between commands and removing several slowdowns that grew quadratically with file size. Per the notes, Mathlib now builds roughly 12% faster than before.
• grind handles more bit-vector and fixed-width integer operations, and treats character literals as numbers.
• bv_decide supports uninterpreted functions through the +uf option (currently for functions returning Bool or BitVec).
• Experimental throws clauses let a def contract state what holds when the function throws.

Please check the breaking changes before upgrading. They include Float min/max, String <, and JSON parsing, which now rejects duplicate keys.

Thanks to Juanjo Madrigal for writing the release highlights.

Full release notes: https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/releases/v4.36.0/

🧠 Terence Tao: Is AI Turning Beautiful Mathematics Into “Toxic Waste”?

In a new interview, Fields Medalist Terence Tao warns that AI-generated mathematical proofs risk prioritizing answers over understanding.

OpenAI reportedly released answers to 722 previously unsolved problems, raising questions about verification, elegance, and mathematical insight.

⚙️ The future of mathematics shouldn't be just AI solving theorems. It should be AI discovering ideas, Lean 4 verifying proofs, and humans understanding the deeper structures.

A correct proof establishes a result. An elegant proof can transform an entire field.

🚀 The real challenge isn't generating more proofs. It's turning AI discoveries into meaningful mathematical knowledge.

Will AI accelerate mathematical discovery or overwhelm researchers with proofs nobody understands?

In formal verification, arguably we do not care about the proofs (as long as they are correct).

In both cases, formulating the actual goal (or theorem) that should be proven remains a task that requires humans (at least for now).
